clinicalPearls: Three goals in the patient with neuropathy: localize the lesion, identify the cause, and determine treatment; the assessment is structured around seven key questions covering systems involved, distribution of weakness, nature of sensory loss, upper motor neuron signs, temporal evolution, hereditary clues, and associated medical conditions (Harrison 22e p.3595).

Pattern recognition is central: length-dependent symmetric distal sensory loss (Pattern 2) points to diabetes/metabolic, drugs, toxins, alcohol, hereditary causes; symmetric proximal AND distal weakness with sensory loss (Pattern 1) is the hallmark of acquired immune demyelinating polyneuropathy (GBS and CIDP); asymmetric/multifocal deficits (Pattern 3, mononeuropathy multiplex) suggest vasculitis, cryoglobulinemia, amyloid, sarcoid, or infection (Harrison 22e p.3596).

Nerve conduction studies and needle EMG distinguish axonal degeneration (low-amplitude potentials, relatively preserved distal latencies and conduction velocities, fibrillations on EMG) from segmental demyelination (slow conduction velocities, prolonged distal latencies, relatively preserved amplitudes, no fibrillations) (Harrison 22e p.3597).

Nonuniform slowing, conduction block, or temporal dispersion on NCS suggests an ACQUIRED demyelinating neuropathy (GBS or CIDP), whereas uniform slowing suggests a HEREDITARY demyelinating neuropathy (e.g., CMT type 1) (Harrison 22e p.3597).

Pure loss of pain and temperature with preserved vibration/position sense, normal strength and reflexes, and normal NCS indicates a small-fiber neuropathy; the most commonly identified causes are diabetes mellitus or glucose intolerance, with amyloid neuropathy also to be considered (Harrison 22e p.3596).

Dramatic proprioceptive/vibratory loss with normal strength, especially when non-length-dependent (arms more than legs or asymmetric), points to a sensory neuronopathy/ganglionopathy (Pattern 9) rather than a typical length-dependent polyneuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3597).

Diabetes mellitus is the most common cause of peripheral neuropathy in developed countries; distal symmetric sensory/sensorimotor polyneuropathy (DSPN) is the most common form, beginning in the toes and ascending (Harrison 22e p.3604).
Diabetic third nerve palsies are characteristically pupil-sparing (Harrison 22e p.3604).
harrison.pathophysiology: Peripheral nerves contain mixed sensory, motor, and autonomic fibers grouped as large myelinated, small myelinated, and small unmyelinated classes; motor axons are usually large myelinated fast-conducting (~50 m/s) fibers, large-diameter sensory fibers carry proprioception and vibration, and small myelinated/unmyelinated fibers carry pain, temperature, and autonomic signals. Disease may target the neuronal cell body (neuronopathy/ganglionopathy), the myelin sheath (myelinopathy/demyelination), or the axon (axonopathy), each producing distinct clinical and electrophysiologic features. Most generalized polyneuropathies are length-dependent axonopathies producing distal (glove-and-stocking) deficits, whereas ganglionopathies produce non-length-dependent loss. Demyelination slows or blocks conduction; axonal loss reduces response amplitudes (Harrison 22e p.3594).
additionalDifferentials: Inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy - Guillain-Barre syndrome (acute) and CIDP (chronic/relapsing) (Pattern 1) (Harrison 22e p.3595)
Cryptogenic/idiopathic sensory polyneuropathy (CSPN) - no etiology found in about half of patients despite extensive evaluation (Harrison 22e p.3595)
Diabetes mellitus and other metabolic neuropathies (DSPN, autonomic, radiculoplexus/Bruns-Garland, mononeuropathies) (Harrison 22e p.3604)
Hereditary neuropathies - Charcot-Marie-Tooth, HSAN, familial amyloid polyneuropathy, SORD neuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3596)
Vasculitic neuropathy presenting as mononeuropathy multiplex (Pattern 3) (Harrison 22e p.3596)
Uremic neuropathy in renal failure (~60% of patients) (Harrison 22e p.3605)
Nutritional/toxic neuropathies (B12, thiamine, alcohol, drugs, chemotherapy, heavy metals) (Harrison 22e p.3611)
Sensory neuronopathy/ganglionopathy - paraneoplastic (anti-Hu), Sjogren's syndrome, CANVAS, cisplatin, vitamin B6 toxicity (Pattern 9) (Harrison 22e p.3596)
Connective tissue/autoimmune disease - rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, scleroderma, sarcoidosis (Harrison 22e p.3605)
infectionMimics: HIV infection - distal symmetric polyneuropathy, AIDP/CIDP, progressive polyradiculopathy, multiple mononeuropathies, sensory ganglionopathy (Harrison 22e p.3606)

Leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae) - most common cause of peripheral neuropathy in Southeast Asia, Africa, and South America; mononeuropathies or symmetric sensorimotor polyneuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3606)
Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi) - facial neuropathy (bilateral in ~half, unlike idiopathic Bell's palsy), polyradiculoneuropathy, multiple mononeuropathies (Harrison 22e p.3606)
Diphtheria (Corynebacterium diphtheriae) - toxin-mediated neuropathy 3-4 weeks after infection (Harrison 22e p.3606)
Other infectious/inflammatory causes producing CSF pleocytosis in suspected GBS/CIDP - HIV, Lyme, sarcoidosis, lymphomatous/leukemic root infiltration (Harrison 22e p.3598)
nonInfectiousMimics: Motor neuron disease (e.g., ALS) - asymmetric distal weakness without sensory loss, especially with upper motor neuron findings (Pattern 5) (Harrison 22e p.3596)
Multifocal motor neuropathy - treatable mimic of motor neuron disease (Harrison 22e p.3596)
Radiculopathy, plexopathy, and compressive/entrapment mononeuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3596)
Neuromuscular junction disorders - myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (Harrison 22e p.3596)
Myopathy, including isolated neck extensor myopathy (Harrison 22e p.3596)

Combined system degeneration - distal sensory signs plus symmetric upper motor neuron involvement from B12, copper, or vitamin E deficiency, severe hepatic disease, or adrenomyeloneuropathy (Pattern 6) (Harrison 22e p.3597)
Critical illness polyneuropathy versus critical illness myopathy in the ICU patient who cannot be weaned from the ventilator (Harrison 22e p.3606)
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and needle EMG to localize (mono- vs polyneuropathy vs radiculopathy/plexopathy) and classify as axonal vs demyelinating (Harrison 22e p.3597)

Autonomic testing (heart rate response to deep breathing, Valsalva, tilt-table, quantitative sudomotor axon reflex) for pure small-fiber or autonomic neuropathy when routine NCS are normal (Harrison 22e p.3597)

Baseline labs: CBC, electrolytes, renal and hepatic function, fasting glucose and HbA1c, thyroid function, B12, folate, ESR, rheumatoid factor, ANA, SPEP with immunofixation, and serum/urine free light chains (Harrison 22e p.3597)
Oral glucose tolerance test in painful sensory neuropathy even when fasting glucose and HbA1c are normal (abnormal in ~one-third) (Harrison 22e p.3597)

Serum free light chains and kappa/lambda ratio (more sensitive than SPEP/immunofixation) and skeletal survey if amyloidosis or monoclonal gammopathy suspected; hematology referral for marrow biopsy (Harrison 22e p.3597)
Vasculitis workup for mononeuropathy multiplex: ANCA, cryoglobulins, hepatitis serology, Lyme Western blot, HIV, occasionally CMV titer (Harrison 22e p.3598)
Lumbar puncture in suspected GBS/CIDP for elevated CSF protein (pleocytosis should be absent in idiopathic cases) (Harrison 22e p.3598)

Antibodies to SS-A/Ro, SS-B/La, and antineuronal nuclear (anti-Hu) antibodies in sensory ataxia/ganglionopathy; nerve biopsy reserved mainly for suspected amyloid or vasculitis and only when NCS are abnormal; skin biopsy for small-fiber neuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3598)
redFlags: Rapidly progressive symmetric proximal and distal weakness with sensory loss (Pattern 1) - acute (GBS) or chronic (CIDP) demyelinating neuropathy; GBS can require respiratory support, so identifying this treatable pattern is critical (Harrison 22e p.3596)
Acute/subacute course (days to weeks) - GBS, vasculitis, diabetic or Lyme radiculopathy require prompt evaluation (Harrison 22e p.3597)
Autonomic dysfunction without diabetes (orthostatic drop without compensatory tachycardia, bowel/bladder/sexual dysfunction) - should raise concern for amyloid polyneuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3595)
Mononeuropathy multiplex pattern - suggests vasculitis and warrants an urgent vasculitis workup (Harrison 22e p.3596)

Severe sensory ataxia from a ganglionopathy - consider paraneoplastic (anti-Hu, often small-cell lung cancer); the neuropathy can precede detection of malignancy and should prompt a cancer search (Harrison 22e p.3598)
harrison.prognosis: Most neuropathies are insidious and slowly progressive; course may be monophasic, progressive, or relapsing (e.g., CIDP, porphyria). Despite extensive evaluation, about half of patients have no etiology identified (cryptogenic/idiopathic sensory polyneuropathy). Outcome depends heavily on cause: treatable acquired demyelinating neuropathies (GBS, CIDP) and treatable systemic causes can respond to therapy, whereas axonal degeneration tends to recover slowly and incompletely. Even with adequate cobalamin replacement, treatment of B12-deficiency neuropathy usually does not fully reverse deficits and at least 50% of patients retain some permanent neurologic deficit (Harrison 22e p.3595, p.3612).
pitfalls: Missing a treatable cause - acquired demyelinating neuropathy (GBS/CIDP) and multifocal motor neuropathy are treatable and should be distinguished from untreatable mimics such as ALS (Harrison 22e p.3596)
Overlooking treatable systemic/metabolic causes such as B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, or a paraprotein/monoclonal gammopathy in an apparently idiopathic polyneuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3597)

B12-deficiency neuropathy can occur with only peripheral findings and without anemia or macrocytosis (lacking in up to 40%); check methylmalonic acid and homocysteine when suspicion is high (Harrison 22e p.3612)

Routine antiganglioside autoantibody panels have no proven added value beyond a complete clinical exam and detailed EDx, and a heavy metal screen is not a useful blind screening test without exposure history or suggestive findings (Harrison 22e p.3598)
Nerve biopsy rarely distinguishes one neuropathy from another beyond clinical exam and NCS; reserve it for suspected amyloid or vasculitis and only when NCS are abnormal (Harrison 22e p.3598)

A hereditary neuropathy can be missed when patients have marked sensory signs but few sensory symptoms plus slowly progressive distal weakness and skeletal clues (high/flat arches, hammer toes, scoliosis); examining family members may be needed (Harrison 22e p.3597)
harrison.severityClassification: No formal numeric severity score is used; characterization is by anatomic/electrophysiologic classification rather than a grading scale - by fiber type affected (motor, sensory, autonomic, or combined; large- vs small-fiber), by distribution (mononeuropathy, mononeuropathy multiplex, polyneuropathy, radiculopathy, plexopathy; ten clinical patterns in Table 457-2), by underlying pathology (axonal degeneration vs segmental demyelination on NCS/EMG, Table 457-3), and by temporal course (acute: days to 4 weeks; subacute: 4-8 weeks; chronic: >8 weeks) (Harrison 22e p.3595, p.3597).
management: Direct treatment at the underlying cause: optimise glycaemic control in diabetes, correct vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, withdraw offending drugs and toxins and abstain from alcohol

Treat immune-mediated demyelinating neuropathy specifically, with intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange for Guillain-Barre syndrome and corticosteroids, immunoglobulin or plasma exchange for CIDP
Relieve neuropathic pain with agents such as gabapentinoids, duloxetine or tricyclic antidepressants
Provide supportive care with foot care, protection of insensate skin, gait aids and physiotherapy or occupational therapy
Manage autonomic features such as postural hypotension and gastrointestinal and bladder dysfunction symptomatically
Complete a structured aetiological work-up with nerve conduction studies and EMG plus metabolic and immunological screening to identify treatable causes
Refer to neurology and provide genetic counselling where a hereditary neuropathy such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is identified
